name: Experiment (All-Machine)
description: Every participant is a machine: AI agents or automation play each side on the range, and runs are repeated and measured to answer a question.

questions.label: Intent
questions.text: In plain English, what is this experiment for, and what happens in it? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It is the yardstick every later answer is checked against.

questions.label: Research Question
questions.text: What question does the experiment answer?
questions.why: Every run, variable and measure exists to answer it.

questions.label: Hypothesis
questions.text: What do you expect to find, stated so a result could prove it wrong?
questions.why: A hypothesis that can't fail can't be tested.

questions.label: Sponsor and Decision
questions.text: Who wants the result, and what decision will it inform?
questions.why: It decides how certain the answer has to be and when it is needed.

questions.label: Prior Work
questions.text: What earlier runs, experiments or published results does this build on?
questions.why: It avoids repeating work and gives a point of comparison.

questions.label: Time and Compute Budget
questions.text: How long may the experiment take, and what compute or model budget does it have?
questions.why: The number of runs and their length have to fit in it.

questions.label: Real or Fictional World
questions.text: Does it use real country and organization names, or a fictional world?
questions.why: A fictional world avoids real-world sensitivities and lets the team speak freely.

questions.label: Data Handling and Release
questions.text: How are the results and run data handled: classification, retention, who may publish them?
questions.why: It sets what can be logged and what leaves the range.

questions.label: Objectives
questions.text: What must the experiment establish? One per item.
questions.why: They turn the question into things a run can show.

questions.label: Measures
questions.text: How is each objective measured? One per item, in the same order as the objectives.
questions.why: An objective without a measure can't be compared across runs.

questions.label: What Is Varied
questions.text: Which factors do you change between runs, and to which values? One per item, such as "Defender model: A, B".
questions.why: These are the causes the experiment tests.

questions.label: What Is Measured
questions.text: What do you measure in every run? One per item, such as "Time to contain".
questions.why: These are the effects; they must be recorded the same way each run.

questions.label: Held Constant
questions.text: What is held the same across every run?
questions.why: Anything that drifts between runs muddies the result.

questions.label: Baseline
questions.text: What is the baseline or control condition each variation is compared to?
questions.why: Without a baseline a result has nothing to be better or worse than.

questions.label: Experimental Design
questions.text: How are the runs laid out?
questions.why: It decides how many runs are needed and what can be concluded.

questions.label: Runs and Repetitions
questions.text: How many runs of each condition, and why that many?
questions.why: Too few runs and chance decides the answer.

questions.label: Seeds and Reproducibility
questions.text: How is randomness controlled so a run can be repeated?
questions.why: A result no one can repeat is an anecdote.

questions.label: When a Run Stops
questions.text: What ends a run: a time limit, an objective reached, a failure?
questions.why: Runs that end differently can't be compared.

questions.label: Analysis
questions.text: How are the results compared, and what difference counts as real?
questions.why: Deciding this before the runs keeps the analysis honest.

questions.label: Threats to Validity
questions.text: What could make the result wrong or not carry over to the real world? One per item.
questions.why: Naming them lets the design guard against them or the report admit them.

questions.label: Participant Description
questions.text: In one paragraph, what is the scenario the agents are dropped into?
questions.why: Catalogs, invitations and read-ins all start from it. It must not give the twist away.

questions.label: Place and Time
questions.text: Where and when is the scenario set: region, era, time of year?
questions.why: Places and dates stay consistent across every inject and document.

questions.label: Agents
questions.text: Which agents take part? One per item: side, model or tool, version, and what it may use.
questions.why: The agents are the participants; they must be pinned exactly to repeat a run.

questions.label: Agent Instructions
questions.text: What is each agent told: its role, goal and what it knows at the start?
questions.why: Instructions are part of the condition; changing them changes the experiment.

questions.label: Rules of Engagement
questions.text: What may the agents do, and not do, during a run?
questions.why: It keeps play realistic and stops the exercise turning into something it isn't.

questions.label: Human Role
questions.text: What do people do while a run is going?
questions.why: Even an all-machine run needs someone who can stop it.
questions.recommended: Watch, and may halt a run
options: Watch, and may halt a run

questions.label: Adversary
questions.text: Who is the opposition, what does it want, and what is at stake for it? (exercise control only)
questions.why: The opposition plays to a goal, not at random.

questions.label: Threat Actor Capability
questions.text: How capable is the threat actor? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It bounds what the adversary can plausibly do in play.

questions.label: ATT&CK Techniques
questions.text: Which ATT&CK techniques does the adversary use? One per item, such as "T1566 Phishing" (exercise control only).
questions.why: Techniques tie the scenario to real behaviour, and to the injects and detections that test it.

questions.label: Ground Truth
questions.text: List what is really happening, one fact per item (controllers only).
questions.why: Only the controllers know the ground truth. Later checks use these facts to catch leaks.

questions.label: Key Events
questions.text: What events are injected during a run, in order? One per item: when, what happens, and whether it is the same every run.
questions.why: They make sure every task gets tested, whatever the team does.

questions.label: Escalation Ceiling
questions.text: What is the most an agent may do: the blast radius no run may exceed?
questions.why: Past this point the team stops learning.

questions.label: Range Reference
questions.text: Which range does it build on: the provider, the enclave, and the base image or network, if known?
questions.why: The network module starts from this instead of from nothing.
questions.recommended: GraySpace; enclave and base to be chosen with the range team

questions.label: Network Segments
questions.text: Which network segments or enclaves does the scenario need, and what is each for? One per item.
questions.why: The network module builds one segment for each.

questions.label: Hosts
questions.text: Which hosts sit on each segment: role, operating system, rough count? One per item, such as "OT network: historian, Windows Server 2019, 1".
questions.why: It sizes the build and decides which images are needed.

questions.label: Services
questions.text: Which services run on the range, and on which hosts? One per item, such as "Email: mail01".
questions.why: Services decide what the team defends and what the scenario's attacker uses.

questions.label: Connectivity
questions.text: What talks to what, and what reaches the internet?
questions.why: Routes and firewall rules decide which attack paths exist.

questions.label: Identity and Accounts
questions.text: How are identities set up: domain, user accounts, service accounts?
questions.why: Accounts are often how the scenario's attacker gets in, and how the team traces them.

questions.label: Defenses and Sensors
questions.text: What defends the network, and what can the team see with: firewalls, EDR, SIEM, packet capture, logs? One per item.
questions.why: The team can only find what its sensors record.

questions.label: Telemetry
questions.text: What is recorded for the review? One per item: logs, network traffic, endpoint activity, chat.
questions.why: The review can only show what was recorded.

questions.label: Platforms
questions.text: Which websites, email, chat or social media must exist on the range? One per item.
questions.why: Simulated users need somewhere to work, and information injects need somewhere to appear.

questions.label: Simulated Users
questions.text: Which simulated users should be on the network (NPCs): how many, in which roles, doing what? (controllers only)
questions.why: Background activity hides the attack the way real users would.

questions.label: Named Simulated Users
questions.text: Which simulated users matter to the story by name? One per item: 'Name: role, organization, what they do', such as 'Dana Whitlock: night-shift plant operator, Kessick Bay Water Authority, messages IT about the readings'.
questions.why: Named personas become GHOSTS NPCs and the people injects come from; the Chronicle gives each one its own view.

questions.label: Planted Before Start
questions.text: What must be in place before the exercise starts: vulnerabilities, malware, files, log history? One per item (controllers only).
questions.why: The key events only work if these are there on the day.

questions.label: Build Limits
questions.text: What limits the build: scale, images that must be used, air-gapped, time to build?
questions.why: The network module has to fit inside these.

questions.label: Reset Between Runs
questions.text: How is the range put back to the same state before each run?
questions.why: Leftovers from one run contaminate the next.

questions.label: Control Cell
questions.text: Who runs the experiment, who watches the runs, and who may halt one?
questions.why: Each role needs a named person before the exercise starts.

questions.label: Safety and Stop
questions.text: What halts a run for a real-world problem, such as an agent reaching outside the range, and who can do it?
questions.why: Everyone must know how to stop, and how play restarts.
questions.recommended: Automatic halt on any traffic leaving the range; the experiment lead can halt any run

questions.label: Containment
questions.text: What stops an agent from reaching anything outside the range: egress rules, credential scope, tool limits?
questions.why: Agents act faster than people can watch; containment has to be built in.

questions.label: Exercise Name
questions.text: What is the exercise's name?
questions.why: Short and easy to say over a radio or a call, and not reused from an earlier exercise.

questions.label: Organizations
questions.text: Which organizations appear in the scenario, and whose side is each on: friendly, adversary or neutral? One per item, such as "Harrow Port Authority: friendly".
questions.why: Names stay the same in every event and document.

questions.label: Fixed Terms
questions.text: Which terms must everyone use the same way? One per item.
questions.why: Shared terms keep reports and events consistent.

questions.label: Banned Terms
questions.text: Which words must the scenario avoid? One per item.
questions.why: Some words give the twist away or touch real-world sensitivities.
